topic: Intro: IT innovation, general-purpose & emerging tech

questions.stem: In Schumpeter's classic framing, what distinguishes innovation from invention?
choices: Innovation requires a patent; invention does not.
Innovation is the first commercial application of an invention.
Innovation must be technologically radical; invention can be incremental.
Innovation is performed by firms; invention is performed by individuals.
questions.explanation: Schumpeter defined innovation as the first commercial application of an invention. Without entering a market, even a brilliant new device remains an invention.

questions.stem: Rogers' diffusion of innovations describes which phenomenon?
choices: The spread of an innovation through a population of adopters over time.
How firms decide to allocate R&D budgets.
The displacement of incumbents by new entrants.
questions.explanation: Diffusion is the temporal spread of an innovation across adopters, classically following an S-curve from innovators through to laggards.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the best example of a process innovation?
choices: Toyota implementing the just-in-time production system.
Lucozade repositioning from a sick-room drink to a sports drink.
Netflix moving from DVD-by-mail to streaming.
questions.explanation: Toyota's just-in-time / lean production reorganised how cars were made, not what was made — the textbook example of process innovation.

questions.stem: Lucozade's shift from a sick-room recovery drink to a sports drink is best classified as which type of innovation?
questions.explanation: The product chemistry barely changed; what changed was the market position. That is position innovation in the 4Ps of innovation.

questions.stem: Henderson and Clark's 'architectural innovation' is dangerous to incumbents because:
choices: It introduces entirely new components they cannot manufacture.
It uses familiar components but reconfigures their interactions, defeating the incumbent's design knowledge.
It targets only the high-end of the market where margins are thin.
It requires regulatory approval the incumbent cannot obtain.
questions.explanation: Architectural innovations keep components but change the system architecture. Incumbents' deep component knowledge becomes irrelevant or misleading.

questions.stem: Which three criteria define a general-purpose technology (GPT)?
choices: Pervades the whole economy, improves over time, and spawns complementary innovations.
Originates in universities, requires standards bodies, and is open-source.
Reduces unit cost, increases speed, and improves quality.
questions.explanation: Bresnahan and Trajtenberg's GPT criteria are pervasiveness, continuous improvement, and innovation spawning. The steam engine, electricity, and the internet all qualify.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT typically listed as a historical general-purpose technology?
questions.explanation: Relational databases are an enabling technology but lack the cross-economy pervasiveness GPT scholars look for. The canonical GPT list is steam, electricity, ICE, computer, internet.

questions.stem: Why did US factory productivity initially fall after the introduction of electricity?
choices: Electricity was unreliable and frequently caused fires.
Workers resisted the new technology and went on strike.
Factories had to be redesigned from line-shaft layouts to per-machine motors, a 40-year reorganisation.
Coal prices spiked, making electricity uneconomic.
questions.explanation: The GPT productivity J-curve: electricity required complete factory redesign. Productivity only surged once unit-drive electrification replaced central line shafts in the 1920s.

questions.stem: The four emerging-tech categories used in this unit are AI/ML; distributed ledger / blockchain; IoT, edge and 5G; and:
questions.explanation: The fourth bucket is long-horizon deep tech: quantum computing, biotech, and advanced materials. The others are either mature (cloud) or sub-domains of AI/security.

questions.stem: A pharmaceutical company files a patent for an mRNA delivery mechanism. They have not yet entered any market. This is best described as:
questions.explanation: Patent filing without commercial entry is invention. Innovation requires first commercial application.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the difference between technology push and demand pull as drivers of innovation?
choices: Technology push originates in universities; demand pull originates in firms.
Technology push starts from a new capability seeking applications; demand pull starts from a market need seeking solutions.
Technology push is faster; demand pull is slower.
Technology push is incremental; demand pull is radical.
questions.explanation: Push = capability looking for a use (e.g. the laser). Pull = customer need driving search (e.g. lithium-ion batteries for portable electronics).

questions.stem: Netflix's transition from DVD-by-mail to streaming to original-content studio is best described as:
questions.explanation: Each step changed Netflix's fundamental business model and mental model. Paradigm innovation is a shift in what the business actually does.

questions.stem: Which Australian innovation challenge is most often cited in this unit?
choices: Strong research output but weak commercialisation and scale-up.
Lack of skilled engineers in absolute numbers.
Excessive government R&D subsidies crowding out private investment.
questions.explanation: Australia's tension: high research quality and per-capita output, weak translation to scaled commercial ventures. Discussed in depth in Week 10.

questions.stem: A scenario reads: 'A startup ships a card that auto-rebalances crypto holdings into stablecoins when spent.' Which emerging-tech category is the primary fit?
questions.explanation: The defining substrate is crypto/stablecoins on a blockchain, so the primary category is distributed ledger, even though AI may feature in rebalancing logic.

questions.stem: Which of these is best characterised as radical innovation?
choices: A faster Intel chip with the same x86 instruction set.
A new colour option for an existing car model.
A software patch that improves battery life.
questions.explanation: mRNA vaccines used a fundamentally different mechanism and unlocked a new industry trajectory — radical. The others are incremental refinements within an existing trajectory.

questions.stem: At the country level, the single most important macroeconomic reason innovation matters is:
choices: It increases trade balance via exports.
It drives productivity growth, the only sustainable source of rising real incomes.
questions.explanation: Long-run growth in living standards comes from productivity growth, which comes from innovation. Trade and patents are downstream effects.

questions.stem: Which is the strongest argument that AI may qualify as a general-purpose technology?
choices: AI startups raise large amounts of venture capital.
AI is pervasive across sectors, is improving rapidly, and spawns complementary innovations (chips, tooling, applications).
AI has been studied since the 1950s, so it is mature.
AI is patent-protected in major economies.
questions.explanation: Apply the three GPT criteria: pervasiveness, continuous improvement, and innovation spawning. AI plausibly satisfies all three.

questions.stem: Which is NOT one of the four types of innovation in the 4Ps framework?
questions.explanation: The 4Ps are Product, Process, Position, Paradigm. Personnel is a distractor.

questions.stem: Which is the best example of incremental innovation?
choices: Replacing the internal combustion engine with electric drivetrains.
A 5% range improvement in a Tesla Model 3 from a new battery chemistry tweak.
questions.explanation: A modest range gain on an existing product is the canonical incremental case. The others are radical/architectural shifts that opened new markets.

questions.stem: A common barrier to innovation that incumbents face but new entrants do not is:
choices: Organisational inertia and commitment to existing customers.
questions.explanation: Incumbents' resource allocation processes optimise for current high-margin customers (foreshadowing Christensen's dilemma). Entrants lack that inertia.

questions.stem: Diffusion of an innovation is typically modelled as which curve?
questions.explanation: Rogers' adopter curve aggregates to a logistic S-curve: slow start, rapid take-off in the middle, saturation at the top.

questions.stem: If a country has high R&D intensity but low high-tech exports, the most likely diagnosis is:
questions.explanation: High R&D, low commercial output is the classic translation gap — the country invents but does not capture the value. Australia's situation.

questions.stem: Which of the following describes the GPT productivity J-curve correctly?
choices: Productivity rises immediately on adoption, then plateaus.
Productivity falls for years while firms reorganise, then surges as complementary innovations diffuse.
Productivity follows a sine wave around a long-term mean.
questions.explanation: GPTs require complementary investments (organisational, human, infrastructural) before benefits show up. Productivity dips, then accelerates.

questions.stem: Which of the following is best classified as an emerging IoT/edge/5G application rather than an AI application?
choices: A network of soil-moisture sensors that throttles irrigation valves in real time.
An LLM that summarises legal contracts.
questions.explanation: Sensor + actuator + connectivity at the edge is canonical IoT. The CV crop case mixes IoT and AI but its primary novelty is the AI model; the soil-sensor case is IoT-first.

questions.stem: The single best one-line definition of innovation for this unit is:
choices: The creation of a novel idea.
The first successful commercial application of an invention.
Continuous improvement of an existing process.
questions.explanation: Schumpeter's definition is the unit's anchor: innovation = first commercial application. Memorise this exact phrasing.
